analysis.one_liner: Repeals the new federal health care law retroactively and substitutes a narrower Republican plan.
analysis.headline: The House Republican bill to repeal the new health care law was referred to eight committees, never got a markup or a vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out the Affordable Care Act and the companion reconciliation law retroactively, restoring the rules that existed before, and then enacted a narrower Republican alternative plan. Repeal would have ended the new coverage subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, protections for people with preexisting conditions, and the taxes that paid for them. The House referred it to eight committees, where it stayed; no committee or chamber ever voted on it, and Congress ended without action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed: employers facing the new employer mandate penalties, higher earners facing the Medicare payroll surtax and investment-income tax, health insurers freed from the law's coverage rules and industry fees, and small businesses facing new taxes. The bill's own findings list $569 billion in tax increases it would have erased and claim the replacement plan would cut average premiums by up to $1,050 a year.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 effective as of their enactment, restoring the prior law.
Enacts the Common Sense Health Care Reform and Affordability Act (H.R. 4038) as introduced in November 2009, a narrower Republican replacement plan.
The bill's findings claim the repeal would eliminate $569.2 billion in tax increases, including employer mandate penalties, and end roughly $110 billion in new health industry taxes.

The bill's findings state that CBO estimated the Republican replacement would cut average premiums by up to $1,050 annually and reduce the federal deficit by $68 billion over ten years, without cutting Medicare.

analysis.who_pays: People who would have gained coverage and protections under the new law: uninsured adults left out of the smaller replacement plan, people with preexisting conditions who could again be denied or priced out of coverage, young adults on their parents' plans, and newly covered Medicaid enrollees.
analysis.who_pays_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

drawbacks.text: Repealing the law retroactively would have stripped away its coverage subsidies, Medicaid expansion, bans on denying people with preexisting conditions, and the other protections that took effect, returning insurance to the pre-2010 rules.

The Republican replacement plan was a much narrower alternative than the law it would have repealed; the bill does not claim it would cover anything close to the number of uninsured people the ACA covered, so the net effect would be large numbers of people losing coverage they had gained.

The bill's own findings acknowledge the pre-repeal alternative relied on allowing insurers to sell across state lines and other market changes rather than broad subsidies, which analysts expected to help mainly people who were healthy and already insurable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For its supporters, the trade was real: end new taxes, employer penalties, and coverage mandates in exchange for a modest, deficit-cutting replacement. For opponents, the cost was severe: millions of people would lose newly acquired coverage and protections so that employers, high earners, and the health industry would pay roughly $569 billion less in taxes. The bill never reconciled that gap — the replacement plan covered far fewer people than the law it repealed — and it never advanced far enough to be amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees and never came out for a vote; the sponsor even filed a discharge petition, a procedure to force a floor vote by collecting member signatures, but Congress ended with no markup and no vote.

narrative.text: Wally Herger introduced the bill on May 27, 2010, with House Republican leaders John Boehner, Eric Cantor, Mike Pence, Kevin McCarthy, and Dave Camp among the original cosponsors.
The House referred it to eight committees: Energy and Commerce, Appropriations, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, and Rules.
In June 2010 portions were referred to subcommittees on Trade and on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, but no committee ever acted on it.
On August 10, 2010, Herger filed a motion to discharge the committees — a petition that would have forced a floor vote if a majority of members signed it — but it did not succeed.
There was no further action; the bill died at the end of the 111th Congress without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who stood to gain coverage and protections under the new health law are better off that repeal never passed: nothing was stripped away, the coverage expansions and insurance rules remained intact, and the taxes funding them stayed in place. Employers, high earners, and the health industry avoided the tax savings they would have realized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People the new health law covered

for.name: Wally Herger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and later filed a discharge petition to try to force a floor vote.

for.name: House Republican leaders (Boehner, Cantor, Pence, McCarthy, Camp)
for.role: Minority leadership and Ways and Means ranking member
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Her chamber referred the bill to eight committees where it stalled; while Democrats held the majority it was never scheduled for a committee vote or a floor vote.

against.name: House Democratic committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the eight committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote in any of the eight committees, despite two subcommittee referrals.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed repealing the health care law he had signed two months earlier and made clear any repeal would not be signed.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors were Republicans; Democrats held 253 of 435 House seats and no Democrat backed the bill, and with the discharge petition failing there was never a floor vote that might have cut across party lines.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from the law's coverage rules and industry fees, but the law also routed new subsidized customers to them and required them to cover everyone; repeal takes those customers back out. Their net interest cut both ways.

Repeal would have eliminated the Medicare payroll surtax and investment-income tax on upper incomes — part of the $569 billion in tax increases the bill's findings cite. Their savings came from taxes that funded coverage for lower- and middle-income families.
Repeal ends the employer mandate penalties the bill's findings put at $52 billion. Employers argued workers paid those costs in wages; workers' interest in guaranteed coverage ran the other way.
Repeal would end the law's fees on the health industry, but the law also extended insurance to millions of paying customers for their products.
Repeal ends the employer mandate and industry taxes the bill says fell on small firms; the counterweight is that their employees would lose the coverage guarantees the law provided.
